content.thinking:
I need to design the phoenix with Genshin-inspired cel-shading, gold filigree, and a pyro elemental glow, with wings spread wide—thinking through realistic proportions like body length and wingspan to make it feel majestic yet grounded.

I'm deciding to have it standing with legs planted on the ground, wings raised and outstretched, and a long trailing tail curving upward so none of the feathers dip below the floor. Now I'm working out the skeleton structure, placing hip, spine, chest, and neck joints along a tilted upward curve to give the body a proud, upright stance.

Head should be its own joint rather than baked into the neck chain's tip, so I'll keep the neck chain to three spans only and add "head" as a separate joint parented to the final neck segment, aimed along its end tangent.

Then I'm adding a "jaw" joint parented to head, positioned using local coordinates. For head orientation I want it tilted slightly down and forward, using the local() helper with forward/up offsets so I don't get confused by the right-hand coordinate convention, and keeping left/right symmetric offsets consistent with the model's mirrored sign convention.

For the wings, I'm planning an arm chain per side (shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand tip), then flight feathers built as individual swept/extruded leaf-shaped parts with a gold-to-orange-to-red gradient and glowing tips, roughly 9 primaries times extra coverage per wing—around 40 feathers per side, staying well within the part and triangle budgets.

Alternatively, I'm weighing using card-based feathers with SVG textures instead—cheaper geometrically since each card is just a few triangles, cut out with alpha, and I can get a cel-shaded flame look with hard color bands rather than smooth gradients. I'll make the flame feathers fully emissive/glowing to read as fire, but keep the wing coverts painted and non-glowing so the shading doesn't flatten out everywhere.

For orientation, I'm figuring out how each feather card should sit in the wing plane: the card's facing axis runs along the feather direction, with "up" as the flow vector so the card lies flat and extends outward, and the width direction comes from crossing the feather direction with up.

I'm deciding to attach each wing segment's cards to its own bone rather than letting them snap to the nearest joint -- primaries to the hand bone, secondaries to the forearm, coverts to the arm -- so each feather group moves rigidly with the right part of the wing.

For individual feather shapes, I want them drawn pointing up toward the tip, with lean 90 and mirror enabled since they're viewed from above. I'm leaning toward making the flame-like feathers glow -- phoenix-style primary and tail feathers with gradient bands from crimson to gold to yellow at the tip -- while keeping the body more cel-shaded for contrast.

Covert feathers stay unlit but visually read as cel-shaded through their painted bands, while flame-tip feathers glow fully bright. I also want flame plume wisps as teardrop cards layered around the body, tail, and wing edges, plus a scattering of small glowing ember diamonds floating nearby for extra fantasy flair.

For the three ornate tail plumes, I'm building them as curved ribbons using a membrane between two offset edge paths rather than a flat extrude, so I can vary width along the length and paint gold edges, red body, flame tips, and eyespot circles directly onto the membrane coordinates.

Working out the width taper function so plumes narrow to pointed tips at both ends, while making sure I avoid zero-width degeneracies that could break the catmull interpolation—clamping to a small minimum width instead.

Tuning the exponent on t to push the width's peak later, toward t≈0.7, so the plume stays fat longer before tapering at the tip.

For the membrane coloring, I'm planning the layout and palette: gold edges, crimson core, warm orange-amber gradient toward the tip, with an eyespot ring near t=0.75–0.9 evoking Genshin's pyro aesthetic with deep crimson, flame orange, and amber tones.

For the eyes, I'm placing stylized anime-style irises on the sides of the bird's head using a decal projection, sized small and tucked into the head sphere, with amber iris color to match the fiery theme.

I'm thinking through how to use cel-shaded paints for the gold decorative flat surfaces without overloading the texture atlas, then moving to lock down the exact geometry carefully, sticking only to API features I'm confident about to avoid mistakes since I'm building this without visual feedback.

Now I'm working out the phoenix's pose: standing on its legs with chest tilted upward, wings spread wide in a rising display with roughly 1.6m length each for a 3.4m wingspan, placing shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints to get a graceful outward-and-up sweep, then extending the primary feathers from the wrist to fan outward and slightly back for the display effect.

Now I'm thinking through the body's overall shape, planning the spine as a loft with stations defining width and height along a chain from the hips upward, aiming for a chunky yet elegant chest form.

Defining the spine joint names and chain structure...

Still defining torso loft stations...

Defining fur paint using cel-shaded coloring based on surface normals for the belly/back contrast, then adding scattered feather cards on the chest to texture the breastplate area.

For the cards, I'm scattering hit points across the body surface and placing feather-shaped cards with bend and lean parameters, using mixed red and orange two-tone feather textures rather than toon shading since cards rely on drawn alpha textures.

Now I'm moving to the wing structure, setting up shoulder joint positions and defining a bone chain running from shoulder through elbow and wrist to the wingtip.

I'm working out the joint naming and span count for the wing chain, deciding whether the hand should be a separate tip joint or folded into the wrist span so primary feathers attach correctly to the right bone before adding a separate digit chain for the primaries.

For the wing plane, I'm setting the leading edge along the arm path with the trailing edge fanning backward, so primary feathers along the hand segment rotate outward from the forward axis toward the back while tilting slightly upward.

I'm laying out feather counts: 9 primaries tapering from 0.95 to 0.7 length, 10 secondaries from 0.65 to 0.5, 4 tertials at 0.4, plus covert rows (primary, greater, median, lesser) decreasing in size along the arm, each grouped by texture to keep mesh calls down to about 6 per wing.

Now I'm working out how each feather card should orient along the flow -- using a frame function that faces the wing's normal direction rather than flattening onto a horizontal plane, so I can introduce proper dihedral tilt by defining the wing plane's normal based on a dihedral angle like 20 degrees.

I'm defining shoulder position and arm segment lengths along the wing's in-plane direction, with the upper arm, forearm, and hand measured out and a slight forward bow at the wrist to match the leading edge sweep.

Calculating elbow, wrist, and hand-tip coordinates from these segment vectors, then extending the primaries outward from the hand base—but the outermost primary tip ends up around x=2.46, giving a wingspan of nearly 4.9 meters, which seems way too large.

Now I'm working out the primary feather placement along the wrist-to-hand line, varying the angle from about 70° near the body down to roughly 8° at the wingtip, with feather lengths tapering slightly between inner and outer positions.

I'm positioning each primary feather base from wrist to fingertip, with outer feathers nearly parallel to the wing direction and inner ones angled back more steeply toward the body, so the leading edge stays covered near the tip.

For secondaries, I'm spacing nine feathers along the elbow-to-wrist line, with angle and length tapering smoothly so the trailing edge flows continuously from the wrist feathers into the elbow feathers without visible gaps.

For a phoenix-like dramatic effect, I'm lengthening the inner secondaries and sweeping them back more as they approach the body, then extending into tertials that merge toward the tail. I'm also setting primary feathers narrow and elongated with small gaps between them so they read as distinct fanned plumes.

With secondaries and primaries overlapping in the same plane, I realize I'll get z-fighting between coplanar cards, so I need to offset each feather layer slightly along the normal direction—alternating small height offsets between neighboring feathers to prevent flickering while keeping the layering visually convincing at the scene's scale.

I'm also deciding to tilt feather cards slightly, shift their root positions back and outward a bit along their length, and keep the card normals double-sided so lighting works from either side. For the flow direction of each feather, I'm flattening it onto the surface plane perpendicular to the frame's normal axis, and setting up the frame function to properly inherit bone transforms when rigid bones are passed in.

Since the feather shapes are left-right symmetric, I decide mirroring doesn't actually matter here, so I'm skipping that concern. Now I'm sketching the SVG outline for the primary feather shape, defining its elongated leaf silhouette with a pointed tip and rounded root using curve paths.

Writing clip-path and gradient bands...

Checking stroke widths render at least 3px at the chosen size, settling on width 3 and a 256–384 texture size within the atlas budget. I'm also mapping out the feather variant set — primary flame band, rounder secondary tip, short covert shield, flame teardrop for plumes, and small body contour feathers.

I'm deciding glow strategy: primaries glow at full strength while secondaries stay matte and textured, treating each card as glowing in its own base color rather than uniformly bright. Now I'm working out how to fill the gap between the wing arm and feather roots with a patagium sweep and layered covert rows — primary coverts sitting just above the primaries along the wrist-to-hand line, and greater secondary coverts running along the elbow-to-wrist base.

I'm placing the covert rows so their bases sit along the arm path itself: one row angled backward covering roughly the first 0.28 of the primaries/secondaries, and a shorter lesser-covert row layered above that, so the arm tube and feather roots are hidden while the visible tips read clearly. I might also add flame wisps along the leading edge or trailing tips later, and I'm starting to think about how the tail streamer plumes should attach via membranes.

For the tail, I'm positioning the root just behind the body and planning five plumes fanned at increasing lateral yaw angles with varying lengths, longest in the middle. I'm defining each plume's centerline as a cubic bezier curve that sweeps backward and outward based on its yaw direction, with control points lifting and spreading the curve to give it a natural trailing, feathery arc.

Now I'm tuning the tip heights so the center plume droops lower while outer plumes curve upward more, making sure every point stays safely above ground level. I'm also working out how to shade each ribbon with a gold edge band before adding the eyespot coloring across its surface.

For the eyespot, I'm defining an elliptical "eye" region with concentric rings -- gold outer, orange/crimson middle, and a cool teal core for contrast -- plus an orange-to-amber gradient near the plume tips to suggest flame.

I'm wrapping the plume paint in a cel shading layer so it reads normals and resolves nested colors using the current surface coordinates, with no fixed shadow override needed.

For membrane thickness, the default width is too thin given the plume's dimensions, so I'm bumping it up to make the mesh visible rather than paper-thin. Then I'm setting up the tail joint chain positions and attaching the plume membranes to follow along the tail bones.

Rather than attaching all plumes to one stiff tail bone, I decide to give each plume its own joint parented to the tail, oriented along the plume's direction, so they can move more naturally as a "fan" role rather than all moving identically together.

For the short tail coverts near the base, I'm thinking of using a set of flat fan cards with flame-colored texture, sized between the plumes, attached to the first tail bone — but I need to figure out the right frame orientation so they droop convincingly rather than floating flat and unnatural above the ground.

Working out the plane normal math so the fan cards tilt downward slightly as they extend back, dropping the tips to roughly y≈0.65 while the body sits at 0.9 — this gives a nicely raised but drooping tail plumage look. Now moving on to the flame plume wisps for the head crest, planning three long crest plumes.

Writing crest ribbon code...

Now sketching the head itself — placing it just past the neck joint at roughly (0,1.72,0.62), orienting a local coordinate frame for the skull parts, and starting the skull as a scaled sphere geometry.

Now I'm shaping the beak as a curved swept bezier path from the head's front down to a pointed hooked tip, keeping the cross-section simple and circular for now rather than adding a custom elliptical taper.

I'm also working out a local head coordinate frame, defining the head's anchor point and a helper function to compute absolute positions as offsets from that anchor, so I can place beak and jaw features consistently relative to the skull.

For the eyes, I'm using surface decals projected onto the skull at specific angles on each side, mirroring for left/right symmetry and sizing them relative to the head's width so they sit naturally into the sphere shape, rigged to the head bone.

For the color scheme, I'm planning a crimson crown fading into amber on the lower face, using a position-based edge blend along the y-axis with jagged teeth detailing for a stylized transition, wrapped in a cel-shading pass.

Now I'm working on the neck geometry: sweeping the neck chain with a tapered elliptical radius, adding a gold scalloped collar loop and feathered ruff cards leaning backward. I'm figuring out which joint point to anchor the collar loop to, settling on using the chain's tangent-facing point at the midpoint rather than a sweep surface point, since that gives the correct axis orientation for the ring.

Given there's no way to verify the model will render without crashing, I'm weighing richness of detail against risk, and deciding to stick with moderately careful, documented call patterns rather than riskier custom geometry. I'm now moving to the legs: setting up a digitigrade bird-leg structure with hip, knee, ankle, and foot joints, defining segment lengths and bend directions so the thigh is mostly hidden in feathers while the tarsus and foot extend forward and back naturally.

So for 3 segments that's 2 inner joints needing 2 bend directions, which clarifies the hint system. For the leg itself, I'm placing the hip and ankle target with roughly 0.76 vertical distance, using segment lengths totaling 0.96 so there's enough slack for the knee to bend forward and the hock to bend back naturally.

Setting up the chain names for hip, knee, ankle, and foot with the foot tip landing at the ankle target, then adding the toe sweeps — three front toes plus one back toe radiating from the ankle point at ground level. I need to account for toe radius so the circular cross-section just touches the floor, which means setting the ankle target height based on that radius offset.

Now I'm building each toe as a short two-point chain parented to the leg, sweeping a tapered cylinder for the digit shape with claw spikes at the tips, spreading the three front toes at yaw angles and placing the back toe opposite.

Styling the feet like golden phoenix armor, with scaled paint over the legs for a cel-shaded amber/gold look and feathered "pants" along the thighs. I'm adding decorative gold anklet rings using a torus geometry oriented around the ankle joint.

I'm skipping a ground plinth or diorama base since the creature should just stand on its talons without extra parts. Instead I'll scatter a few small floating glowing ember shapes near the base as a subtle flame effect, keeping them minimal so they don't look like stray loose geometry.

Now I'm figuring out the chest ornament—a gold-framed teal gem like a vision crystal, placed by raycasting forward from a point near the chest onto the body surface to find the correct attachment position.

I'm also thinking about adding a gold gorget necklace with ornate filigree and hanging tassels from the chest gem, maybe three cords dangling downward for that Genshin-style decoration.

Beyond that, I want gold bracers at the wrists with gems and tassels, golden cuffs at the wing tips, filigree borders on the wing coverts, and gold rachis lines on the feathers. Topping it off, I'm picturing a tiara-style headdress with a gold crest ornament on the forehead.

I should also add a small golden claw spike at the wrist's leading edge for a thumb-claw accent. Now I'm counting up the joint hierarchy: spine segments plus hip root, neck joints, head, jaw, plume chains, tail segments, and the leg joint chains down to the toe tips.

Adding wing joints brings the total well under the 160 limit, so I'm now working out how to assign the primary and secondary feather groups to specific bone spans—secondaries on the elbow-to-wrist segment, primaries on the wrist-to-hand segment, with a final hand-tip segment for the wingtip feathers.

Writing feather grouping helper...

I realize card sizing is uniform per batch call, but primary feathers vary significantly in length, so I may need to call cards per-feather instead of batching, since a single uniform size won't capture that variation.

Since each wing has roughly 40 parts and there are two wings, calling cards per feather yields around 80-100 parts total, which is well within budget, and calls themselves are cheap. Materials can still be shared per texture and tint, so this approach stays efficient while handling layered offsets and flow direction correctly.

For the curl, I want primaries to flick upward at the tips rather than droop, so I should use a negative bend value with lean at 90 degrees — negative bend curls toward the normal (upward) rather than further along the flow direction, giving a nice upward flick with minimal extra geometry cost.

Now I'm sizing the feather cards so their width-to-length ratio roughly matches each texture's aspect ratio, then sketching out the texture generator functions — a flame feather primary with banded colors from crimson base through orange, amber, to yellow tips with gold edges, and a broader rounded secondary feather outline with its own banding and a gold edge stripe.

Defining more feather shapes...

Core colors with amber glow, used on tail plume tips, crest, and wing tips. For the tassel piece, I'm defining a hanging gold cap with cord and red tassel strands, noting the viewBox orientation so the root sits at top and the card reads correctly when viewed from downstream with a 180-degree lean.

So I draw the tassel upside down in its own frame—cap near the drawing's bottom edge, strands reaching toward the top—so once hung, the root attachment lands at the top and strands fall downward correctly.

Now I'm setting up imports and builder utilities for the scene, being careful to only import what's actually used since unused imports fail typecheck, and starting to define the color palette constants...

Defining more palette colors...

Setting up the painted color variants and skeleton joint hierarchy...

Building the spine and neck chains with catmull curves...

Adding jaw joint and tail chain...

I'll set plume bases parented to tail2 joint since the tip extends beyond -0.5, then start defining wing points per side using an angle offset.

Still writing wing chain...

Arm feathers use crimson coloring with gold cuff rings at elbow and wrist for accent. I'm computing the wing surface normal and working out the feather lay function to orient each feather along the wing curvature.

Writing feather placement logic...

Working out the wrist/hand boundary at roughly 56% along the arm, then checking the base points against the arm's curve path and setting up layering offsets so inner fingers render on top.

Now mapping the secondary feathers from west to east with increasing angle (70° to 98°) and gradually shortening lengths, layering them slightly above the primaries so the two sets overlap naturally near the wing's middle.

I'm checking for z-fighting where primary and secondary bases nearly coincide near the wrist, resolving it by assigning distinct height layers—primaries lower, secondaries just above, coverts higher still. Then I'm working out the tertials, placing their bases closer to the shoulder with angles around 100-106°, while making sure they don't collide with the body's loft width near the shoulder region.

For the covert layers, I'm defining greater primary coverts and greater secondary coverts with specific base positions, lengths, widths, and texture assignments so they visually cover the hidden roots of primaries and secondaries, leaving the outer 0.3-0.8 span of primaries exposed as intended. Now I'm starting on the lesser coverts as a second row to fill in the remaining gaps.

Adding lesser coverts row...

I'm tallying the total card count per wing across primaries, secondaries, tertials, and all coverts (~52 cards, 104 per bird) to confirm it stays within reasonable triangle/part budgets, then planning flame wisp accents at each primary tip standing upright off the wing plane with a cross layout and glow, leaning back along the flow direction.

I'm extending wisps to secondary tips with varied sizes, then moving to the body shape — lofting a sequence of stations from tail base to chest, bound to the spine bone, with fur-edge cel shading transitioning from crimson to amber for the pelt texture.

Now I'm scattering body contour feather cards across the surface, filtering out underside normals, sizing them small and leaning them back-down to follow the surface flow toward the tail.

Now I'm setting up the neck with its own sweep and chain path, scattering smaller feather cards up along it, and adding a gold collar torus near the base for detail.

Adding a ring of feather-like gold ruff cards around the neck base, leaning back and flowing downward so they radiate outward naturally.

Now shaping the skull as a scaled sphere with a crimson-to-amber gradient face, then starting to plot the beak shape as a curved path from the face forward and down.

Still shaping jaw and crest geometry...

Placing the crown shape at the skull-top position, I'm working out the gold cel-shaded color and thickness for extrusion, then double-checking how the outline's origin point relates to the crown's z-offset.

For the crest, I'm sketching three ribbons sweeping back from the crown using bezier paths that curve downward and backward in the vertical plane, with tapering widths and bone-colored heads.

Writing ribbon helper function...

Checking the edge arrays for building the membrane shape—computing both sides as offset points along the path, then considering whether to smooth them with a catmull curve before passing to the membrane function.

Defining plume layouts with yaw, length, tip position, and width parameters for each plume.

I'm working out the bezier curve path for the plume, with the middle control point arching upward before sagging toward the tip height.

Checking the end tangent direction from p2 to p3, it's mostly horizontal with a moderate drop, which works fine for the ribbon's normal calculation. Now I'm wondering whether the plume tips should curl upward at the end for a more natural look.

Tail base ruffle uses an 11-card fan at the second tail joint. Now I'm working out the leg geometry, computing hip and ankle positions for each side and generating limb points with bend directions...

Writing limb code...

I'm realizing the chain function likely accepts the point array directly as a polyline, so I'll pass the four points straight to the chain builder with four joint names (hip, knee, ankle, foot) so the ankle target becomes the tip foot joint, matching the pattern from the docs where three names leave no tip but four names do.

Setting up contact and parenting...

The shadow approach works for gold-orange scaly legs. For thigh feathers, I'm scattering small pant-like cards near the upper thigh region of the leg sweep, sizing and leaning them to layer over the body texture, though I need to check that the sweep type is accepted properly.

Now I'm figuring out the leg joint indices to place an anklet: tracing hip, knee, ankle, and foot-tip joints to locate the tarsus segment, then positioning a gold torus ring partway down it with a slightly larger radius than the leg itself, plus adding a second gold greave ring higher up near the knee-hock area.

For the toes, I'm computing three forward toe tips plus a rear hallux by offsetting from the foot point at splayed yaw angles and varying lengths, then tapering their radius from base to tip so the lowest points barely graze or sit just above the floor within the allowed tolerance.

Checking the toe tip stays near y≈0, confirming the lowest point of the model sits essentially at ground level with height roughly 2.0. Now I'm setting up the toe joint chains, attaching each toe to the foot tip with proper naming per side.

Writing sweep and spike calls...

I'll skip extra knuckle/pad details and verify the foot hex point reuses the ankle position correctly, then move to the tail: sweeping a tapered tube along the tail chain in crimson with a gold ring band.

Now I'm computing the tail fan cards — 11 flat panels spread across angles with directions derived from a tilt angle, checking that each card's spread direction stays perpendicular to its lean normal, then noting mid-angle plumes will overlap and planning the tail fan's texture coloring.

Writing SVG flame path...

Adding glowing ember octahedra near the wings, attaching them to fixed points on the hips bone for subtle animated highlights.

I'm placing a gem pendant on the chest with two tassels hanging below it, figuring out the chest surface position to anchor everything relative to the body's front-facing coordinates.

The belly curves backward below the gem, so the hanging tassel would float slightly in front like a real ornament—that's fine. I'll place a couple tassels offset in x, rooted to the spine joint, and skip the full necklace sweep in favor of the existing collar rings at the neck, then add gold ornaments at the wing points.

Now I'm placing a bracer ring at the wrist with a gem on top glowing teal, adding hanging tassel cards beneath the wing anchored to the wrist joint, and finishing with a gold claw spike at the tip angled forward and outward.

For the shoulder area, I'm adding a gold scalloped pauldron where the wing meets the body, using a hemisphere oriented along the outward normal and scaled flat, plus considering a gold gorget or collar for extra ornamentation.

I'm pulling in the toon shading kit (cel, fur edges, zigzag, anime eyes) and glow helpers for the materials, then working out the vertical proportions—wing tip height, primary feather extension, and head/crest top—based on the body's joint offsets and bend angles.

Overall the creature comes out to roughly 2 meters tall with a 3.8 meter wingspan and about 2.5 meters of body-to-tail depth, which I'll verify against the preview later. For the feathers, I'm writing an SVG generator function that builds layered card textures with base and highlight colors, scaled up 1.6x so stroke widths stay crisp at the target resolution.

Still writing feather paths...

Still writing feather SVG paths...

Still writing zigzag path logic...

Now I'm planning a generic feather SVG function that takes dimensions, an outline path, colored bands with depths, and base/edge colors, plus an optional rachis (the central shaft, colored gold with a thicker stroke) and optional decorative gold dots for secondary feathers. For covert feathers I'm sketching band colors—crimson base with an orange scalloped ring near the edge.

I'm designing two covert variations (red/orange and orange/amber) using layered ellipses clipped to the outline, a thick gold stroke, and a short gold rachis line, then reusing this same texture at a smaller scale for body feathers. I'm also reconsidering the card proportions since coverts need a taller, more elongated viewBox than the current aspect ratio allows, so I'm redefining the outline path to stretch the feather shape vertically.

Now I'm working through the tassel orientation — since the card is drawn root-at-bottom but gets positioned hanging downward, the drawing effectively appears flipped to the viewer, meaning the knot/cap ends up rendered near the top rather than the bottom. I need to account for this inversion when positioning the strands and attachment point.

Writing SVG code...

Adding the gold fringe band, then setting up the Genshin-style eye with amber iris color and the decal placement logic that positions it on the skull surface using a hit-test around point.

Checking that the hit's normal direction and default orientation work correctly for the eye decal, then deciding to skip beak nostrils and cheek patches for now. I'm considering adding a dorsal flame crest or mane along the neck and spine using crossed flame-wisp cards.

Sampling points directly along the neck sweep's dorsal angle rather than relying on a callback-based `along` helper, then placing flame cards at each frame with lean and flow settings for a windswept look...

I'm applying the same body-sweep sampling approach along the spine for a mane of fire wisps from head to tail, confirming `glow()` wraps the resulting mesh array correctly, and checking the membrane and joint signatures take Catmull-rom paths and Vector3 anchors as expected for the wing trim and tail plumes.

Now I'm estimating total part counts across body, wings, legs, and tail feathers to stay around 300 meshes, watching for z-fighting between layered coverts, and double-checking I'm not shadowing the imported `frame` function with a local variable while building fan frames off the tail joints.

For the body surface scatter I'm checking the filter signature receives a Hit with normal data, then moving to the neck ruff ring—using the chain's frame at a given t, generating card items with size, lean, and flow parameters, and deriving the bone weighting from the ring's joints before setting up the gold torus ring geometry.

Now I'm finalizing the color palette (crimson, red, orange, amber, gold variants, teal, beak and claw tones) and sketching out the helper functions inside the build closure for adding feathers and other parts.

Writing import statements...

I'm double-checking that each imported utility—Joint, INK, zigzag, furEdge, cel—actually gets used somewhere, like INK for eyespot rings and zigzag for the plume paint pattern, so nothing ends up as dead code.

Now I'm sketching the SVG helper that generates a zigzag region path based on width, depth, and tooth count, then starting to define the band types for the texture layers.

Writing feather texture SVG...

Still defining feather textures...

Checking the ellipse overlaps confirms the layering works, so I'm defining variant pairs like COV_A and COV_B with different color combinations, plus flame wisp and tassel shapes at consistent sizes. Now I'm starting the main export function...

Writing paint definitions...

Still writing flame zigzag thresholds...

I'm also computing the eye ellipse dimensions in real-world scale based on the along-length and width proportions.

I'll color the crest with a simple threshold-based shader splitting it into crimson, orange, and amber bands. Now moving on to defining the skeleton joints for hips, spine, neck, and jaw, computing head position first so the jaw can reference it, then building the body loft along the spine bones.

Writing skull geometry and beak sweep...

Still shaping the beak geometry... now adding the jaw mass as a scaled sphere with amber coloring, then starting on the crown tiara extrusion with its own outline.

I'm placing a gem on the tiara using an octahedron geometry, working out the exact coordinates for where it should sit on the crest's front point and side faces relative to the head bone.

I'm figuring out where to anchor the three crest ribbons at the back of the crown, calculating their base positions against the skull's curvature so they attach naturally near the tiara's rear edge.

For each ribbon's yaw angle, I'm computing a curved path that arcs upward then droops downward, and checking that the ribbon's cross-section stays properly vertical by verifying the cross product between the ribbon's direction and its horizontal normal gives a vertical vector. Now I'm setting the ribbon width.

I'm writing a helper function that builds two edge curves for a ribbon by walking along a path, computing the tangent at each point, finding the perpendicular "side" vector via cross product with the ribbon's normal, and tapering the width using a sine curve so it narrows toward the tip. I'm verifying the side vector doesn't flip sign unexpectedly for tail plumes, then checking what `path.at(t)` actually returns based on how it's used elsewhere.

Confirming the path and tangent functions return proper Vector3 objects compatible with the catmull spline builder, and double-checking the joint indexing for the wing chain (shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand) matches the five-point span structure. Now I'm setting up the wing-building loop, defining dihedral angle vectors for the up and normal directions on each side.

Adding feather direction and placement logic...

Still writing wing glow and wisp placement logic...

Setting lean angle to 25 with flow leaning outward per feather, sizing the cards, and mapping flow as a per-index direction function. Now moving on to building the secondaries loop...

Writing secondary feather positions...

Adding tertial feathers...

Checking that the body tapers enough near the tail to avoid clipping with the tertials confirms no intersection there. Now I'm moving on to defining the primary coverts positions along the wing.

Writing coverts layout...

I still need to add tertial coverts along the upper arm, then consider the leading edge geometry where the arm tube meets covert bases, plus plan the ornamentation details like a pauldron, bracers, gems, tassels, and thumb claw.

For the pauldron, I'm building a hemisphere shape positioned at the shoulder joint oriented along the wing's normal direction, with a gold rim torus around its edge to give it a decorative trim.

Now I'm working out the arm details: a bracer torus at the wrist, an octahedron gem mounted above it, and an elbow ring oriented toward the shoulder. I'm also attaching a hanging tassel from beneath the wing at the wrist, checking that it ends well above the floor.

Now I'm adding a thumb claw spike, confirming the paint/fill overload works, then setting up the tail fan geometry with angled spokes radiating from a base bone.

Still writing fan code...

I'm checking that the fan's tilt and arc interact nicely with the plumes above, with the fan dipping below at its tip while plumes arch over the center before descending — a layered visual mix.

Now I'm adding glowing wisp cards at the plume ends oriented along the path tangent, a crimson tail tube with a gold ring accent, and fire-wisp card clusters along the back and neck sweep with randomized flow and size variation for a glowing mane effect.

Next I'm scattering body cards away from the chest gem, setting up the neck sweep ring geometry and ruff positions, placing eye decals, and generating ember particles scattered above the hips using small glowing octahedrons in orange, amber, and yellow with randomized scale and rotation.
